lines: A nightly reconciliation between the source and the warehouse is off by a handful of rows.
That gap is exactly what makes this bug dangerous: nothing about it looks like a failure.
A cursor only ever checks whether it ran, never whether what it read was the whole truth, so a row can vanish from its view while every dashboard still shows green.
Here's the question before I show you where.
An incremental cursor built on a last-modified column only ever asks for rows newer than wherever it last stopped.
So what kind of change, however you tune that cursor, can it simply never catch?
answer: A row updating twice inside the same run looks like the dangerous case, but it isn't — re-reading an unchanged row is exactly what a safe, repeatable merge is built to shrug off.
A row deleted outright is the real blind spot. There's no column left on it to compare against anything, because there's no row left at all.

lines: Here's the mechanism underneath that blind spot, and it's subtler than a simple deletion.
A transaction's own notion of 'now' is fixed the moment it starts, and never moves again for as long as that transaction stays open.
So a transaction that starts early, works slowly, and only commits much later still stamps its row with that early starting moment — not with whenever it actually finishes.
An application server that stamps its own rows by hand runs into the same family of trouble for a much plainer reason: its clock simply disagrees with its neighbours'.
I ran this directly against a real database rather than just describing it.
While that slow transaction sat open, a cursor run looked for new rows, found none, and still pushed its own watermark forward anyway.
The transaction then committed, carrying a timestamp from before that watermark moved. Every strict run after that point looks for something newer than the watermark and simply never finds it again.
The same disagreement shows up again in a completely different kind of cursor.
A database sequence hands out a number and never takes it back, even if the transaction that asked for it rolls back entirely.

So a transaction that grabbed its number early but commits late can still land behind one that grabbed a later number and committed sooner. The ordering you'd expect from the numbers and the order things actually commit in can simply disagree.
Here's the fix, and I ran it for real too.
Re-reading a short margin of time behind the watermark, instead of stopping exactly at it, picks that missed row straight back up.
And because the way it's written back in keys off that row's own identity rather than blindly inserting, running that same re-read three times over left the row exactly as it was. Once.
One more thing before moving on: how wide does that margin actually need to be?
Exactly as wide as the slowest transaction this particular source ever runs, measured, not guessed at.
Pick anything shorter, and you've simply recreated the same blind spot you were trying to fix, just with smaller numbers.
Now the one failure none of this actually repairs.
A row that gets deleted outright leaves nothing behind. No timestamp, no trace, nothing at all for any query to compare against a watermark.
Widen that lookback margin as far as you like. There's simply no signal left in the data for it to find.
So: four separate ways a cursor like this can miss a row, and I reproduced every one of them for real.
Lookback paired with a safe, repeatable write-back fixes three of those four completely.
What's left isn't just one stubborn case. Any source whose transactions run long enough, or whose in-between states actually matter, has already outgrown what a cursor like this can promise.
That's not a dead end, it's a handoff. Reading a database's own change log directly, rather than polling a column after the fact, is built to cover exactly the ground a cursor can't.
One more case, run for real against the database directly, bypassing the application layer entirely.
A bulk update changes a whole batch of rows but never touches their last-modified column at all. Does the next cursor run catch any of it?
answer: It doesn't, and the reason is almost embarrassingly simple: that column only ever changes because something explicitly wrote a new value into it.
Skip writing it, and you've recreated the exact same blind spot as an outright deletion — a real change sitting in the table with absolutely no timestamp announcing that it happened.
